The paper describes a benchmark for evaluating sensitive information recognition (SIR) models. This includes a categorization of possible SI types; a series of transformations to test the robustness of the models; and an evaluation of both "classic" NLP models and state of the art LLMs with various prompts. The reviewers agree that the contributions are valid, correct, and in line with the D&B track.

With a touch of sadness, I note that the review process for this manuscript has been unsatisfactory, despite several reminders and flags on all sides. In particular:

* Reviewer 2gBL provided a single, very vague concern (concerning country codes) and completely ignored the rebuttal. I did not consider this review in my final evaluation, leaving three borderline accept (4, 4, 4) scores.

* Reviewer LNBd had several concerns, mostly notably the use of a single metric (accuracy) to evaluate the results and the lack of contextual information for LLMs (e.g., to distinguish a patient's name from a doctor's name). There was very limited interaction during the rebuttal, although the score was raised by one point. This point is discussed at length in the limitation section of the paper.

* Reviewer oPCC was not convinced by the realism of the adversarial transformations, but the rebuttal appears to have addressed this issue. 

* Reviewer iWiq stated that "likely algorithmic approaches [exist] specifically designed to tackle this proble (sic)". However, the reviewer failed to provide examples and did not engage in the rebuttal, making this issue unaddressable.

Overall, while this is slightly outside my own area of expertise, I find the paper well written and the results interesting. The limitations are clear and the code appears to be accessible and reproducible. Since no significant concerns remain, and since the benchmark provides a valuable contribution to the field, I lean toward acceptance for the D&B track.

===== FINAL UPDATE FROM DB Track PCs ====

The final decision for this paper has been taken by the program chairs after consultation with the SACs. All Senior Area Chairs have ranked papers according to the feedback from the AC during the review process. We decided to leave the original meta-review to reflect the opinion of the AC in light of the initial discussions with reviewers and SAC.

In this “Author Final Remarks”, R1, R2, R3 and R4 are used to denote reviewers 2gBL, LNBd, oPCC and iWiq, respectively. We sincerely appreciate all reviewers’ constructive feedback and are encouraged by their recognition of the following **strengths**.
- **Valuable and Diverse Benchmark**: **DataSIR** is a benchmark for sensitive information recognition (SIR) in **real-world data leakage** scenarios [R1, R2, R3, R4], being **multilingual** [R1], **regulation-aligned** [R1, R3, R4], and supporting diverse **format transformations** [R1, R2, R3, R4], enriching the diversity of sensitive data.
- **Comprehensive Evaluation**: Covers traditional NLP pipelines and modern LLMs under varying prompt informativeness, demonstrating strong differentiation capability [R1, R2, R3, R4].
- **Readability and Reproducibility**: Highly readable [R2, R3], with dataset and code fully open-sourced and detailed implementation descriptions [R2].

While there are still some misunderstandings in “Limitations Weaknesses”, we try the best to address them in the following.
- **No introduction of new detection methods** [R2]: This work adheres to the standards of the *Datasets and Benchmarks Track*, aiming to provide a high-quality, publicly accessible benchmark for model evaluation under complex format transformation conditions.
- **Insufficient inclusion of cross-country samples** [R1]: In addition to mobile numbers (Lines 121–126), samples of Personal ID, Landline Number, Driver’s License, Passport, Postcode, and other cross-national identifiers have been added.
- **Neglecting contextual information** [R2]: While context-based SIR is highly valuable, this work—focused on rigor and scope—first establishes a context-free baseline as a reference, with the integration of contextual information explicitly identified as future work.
- **Design of format transformations** [R3]: Additional empirical evidence has been provided to show that these transformations originate from real-world evasion strategies.

Additionally, following the reviewers’ suggestions, we incorporated **Precision**, **Recall**, and **F1-score** metrics [R2], refined the manuscript for some writing problems [R4], and listed model parameter settings to facilitate reproducibility [R4].

Our sincere gratitude is once again extended to all reviewers for their valuable feedback, and we hoped that **DataSIR** will serve as a foundation for further research and foster deeper exploration in the field of SIR.

rebuttal.value:
Thank you for your insightful and encouraging comments. We carefully and thoroughly revised the manuscript to address all the comments. The detailed point-to-point responses are provided as follows.

**Limitations Weaknesses 1:**  

The paper primarily aggregates existing transformation techniques without introducing fundamentally new detection methods or modeling strategies.

**Response to "Limitations Weaknesses 1":** 

We sincerely thank you for your thorough review and insightful comments. You have accurately identified that the primary focus of our work lies in constructing a benchmark rather than proposing a novel recognition algorithm, and we fully agree with your observation.

First, we would like to clarify the positioning of our work. Our submission strictly adheres to the first criterion of the “Datasets and Benchmarks Track”:

> New datasets, or carefully and thoughtfully designed (collections of) datasets...
>

Our core contribution lies precisely in this aspect: we present a high-quality, publicly available benchmark designed to evaluate model recognition capabilities under complex format transformations. Experimental results across various NLP models and LLMs further validate the effectiveness of this benchmark. We believe that, at the current stage of research, the construction of such an “infrastructure” is itself a valuable and independent contribution to the community.

We emphasize that constructing a rigorous benchmark and proposing a novel algorithm are two equally important yet distinct research endeavors. Building on this validated dataset, we plan to explore and propose novel adversarial recognition algorithms in future work.

Once again, we sincerely appreciate your valuable feedback, which has been instrumental in helping us articulate the significance of our work and shape our future research direction. We hope this clarification helps convey the core contribution of our study.




**Limitations Weaknesses 2:**  

Evaluation focuses solely on recognition accuracy (LRAcc/DRAcc), without considering precision-recall balance, error types, or robustness curves.

**Response to "Limitations Weaknesses 2":** 


Thank you for your valuable suggestion. In the original version of the manuscript, we employed LRAcc/DRAcc to highlight the model's recognition and recovery performance across different sensitive data categories, from the perspective of dataset construction. However, we acknowledge that this metric does not capture the trade-off between precision and recall, nor does it adequately reflect the risk of false positives and false negatives in real-world deployments.

To address this limitation, we have supplemented our analysis by reporting the Precision, Recall, and F1-score of the Gemini model across different sensitive data categories, along with a fine-grained performance analysis. Due to space constraints in the rebuttal, we present a subset of the results as shown in the table below:

Table 1. Performance Metrics by Sensitive Data Categories (Partial)

| Category        | Precision (%) | Recall (%) | F1-score (%) |
|----------------|---------------|------------|---------------|
| IMEI           | 26.03         | 21.87      | 23.77         |
| IMSI           | 83.33         | 6.67       | 12.35         |
| MAC            | 62.77         | 89.23      | 73.70         |
| Mobile Number  | 27.47         | 80.31      | 40.94         |

As shown in the table, the recognition performance varies significantly across different sensitive data categories. For example, IMSI achieves relatively high precision but suffers from extremely low recall, resulting in a substantially reduced F1-score. This indicates a tendency to misclassify IMSI as other numeric entities such as IMEI or Mobile Number. In contrast, the F1-score for MAC exceeds its precision, suggesting that false positives may originate from similar entities.

In future work, we plan to incorporate more comprehensive evaluation dimensions, including a balanced analysis of precision and recall, cost modeling for false positives/negatives, and robustness assessment at the category level. These efforts aim to better align our evaluation framework with practical deployment needs, especially for enhancing controllability and reliability in high-risk scenarios.


**Limitations Weaknesses 3:**  

All samples are presented as isolated phrases, ignoring critical context that often determines sensitivity.

**Response to "Limitations Weaknesses 3":** 

We sincerely appreciate your insightful comments. We fully agree that in real-world scenarios, context is a decisive factor influencing the performance of sensitive information recognition (SIR).

We recognize that “context-aware sensitive information recognition” is itself a complex and highly valuable line of research. Therefore, to ensure the rigor and focus of the current study, we made a deliberate decision to first establish a baseline for SIR in a context-free setting. We believe that such a baseline serves as a necessary reference point for all future work incorporating contextual signals. As noted in the “Conclusion and Future Work” section of our paper, integrating contextual information is a clearly identified direction for our subsequent research.

To demonstrate that this choice reflects a deliberate research plan rather than a neglect of the issue, we would like to share some representative challenges that must be addressed when exploring context-aware SIR:

1. Multidimensionality: Context goes far beyond surrounding text; it includes syntactic structures (e.g., "My Mobile Number is...") and semantic domains (e.g., "medical records" vs. "code discussions").

2. Varying cue strength: Contextual cues range from strong prompts ("Please enter your 18-digit Personal ID") to weak or implicit signals, and even entirely absent hints.

3. Adversarial use: Context may be deliberately manipulated to deceive models—for instance, disguising sensitive data as “product serial numbers,” or using prompt injection to suppress detection.

Addressing these challenges requires the construction of a large-scale, high-quality, and dedicated dataset, which constitutes a substantial and independent engineering effort. We believe that merging this broader agenda with the current work—focused on establishing a fundamental recognition benchmark—would dilute the depth and clarity of both contributions. Thus, we chose to first resolve the foundational problem, thereby laying the groundwork for more sophisticated context-aware research in the future.

Once again, thank you for your valuable feedback. It has further reinforced our determination to prioritize “context-aware sensitive information recognition” as a key direction in our future work.

**Limitations Weaknesses 4:** 

The 21 format transformations are treated uniformly, without a structured taxonomy based on semantic preservation, reversibility, or attack complexity. 

**Response to "Limitations Weaknesses 4":** 

In response to your suggestion regarding “establishing a structured categorization of transformation types to analyze model failure modes,” we conducted additional experiments. Specifically, we introduced the n-gram-based Jaccard similarity between the original and transformed text to quantify the complexity of each format transformation, and assessed the recognition performance of an LLM (Gemini) using the Micro F1-score. A subset of the results is presented below:

Table 2. Impact of Format Transformations on Semantic Similarity and Recognition Performance (Partial)

| Type                        | Avg. 3-gram Jaccard Similarity (%) | Micro F1-Score (%) |
|-----------------------------|------------------------------------|---------------------|
| Inserting special characters| 53.51                              | 66.02               |
| URL encoding                | 36.20                              | 86.02               |
| Base64 encoding             | 0.00                               | 59.02               |
| Octal                       | 0.00                               | 18.00               |

We found that the complexity of a format transformation does not exhibit a simple linear relationship with model performance. Instead, the recognition capability of the model is mainly influenced by two factors:

1. Familiarity with transformation logic: Compared to irregular, noise-like transformations such as Inserting special characters, which may increase complexity but resemble training noise, the model performs significantly better on structured transformations like URL encoding.

2. Feature salience of the transformed output: The model can effectively recognize transformations with distinctive patterns, such as Base64 encoding, but struggles with transformations like Octal, which lack clear and distinguishable characteristics.

These findings offer valuable insights into the failure modes of LLMs. We will incorporate this analysis into the revised manuscript and include additional metrics for deeper investigation.

Please let us know if these additions address your concerns. Thank you again for taking the time to review our work and for offering such constructive feedback.

Thank you for your insightful and encouraging comments. The paper has been carefully and thoroughly revised to address all the points raised. Detailed, point-by-point responses are provided as follows.

**Limitations Weaknesses 1:** 

some mistakes in writing, such as  Line 86-88 and Line 271.

**Response to "Limitations Weaknesses1":** 

Thank you for your careful comments. We have addressed the issues in our revision and revised other similar or related mistakes accordingly. We sincerely appreciate your meticulous review.

**Limitations Weaknesses 2:**

I would consider increasing the score if the following issue is addressed:

The current version only evaluates existing open-source packages and models (both open- and closed-source). However, there are likely algorithmic approaches specifically designed to tackle this problem. Including a discussion of related algorithmic methods, along with corresponding evaluation results, would significantly strengthen the paper.

**Response to "Limitations Weaknesses 2":**

We sincerely appreciate your valuable suggestion. We fully agree that incorporating comparisons with dedicated algorithmic approaches would further strengthen the validity and impact of our work. In response, an additional round of in-depth literature review was conducted. However, we found that no existing specialized algorithms are directly and fairly comparable with the general-purpose models we evaluated in an end-to-end (out-of-the-box) setting.

Several related works were identified, but substantial differences in scope and design render a direct comparison infeasible for the following reasons:

1. Mismatch in core research objectives:  
These studies do not aim to detect transformed text in downstream applications, but rather focus on robustness theory or benchmark design.  
    - Focus on adversarial robustness: Works such as ALUM [1] and TAVAT [2] aim to improve intrinsic model robustness under white-box attacks by injecting gradient-based perturbations into embedding spaces. This significantly differs from our goal, which is to evaluate black-box detection performance under realistic format transformations.  
    - Designed as benchmarks, not detection methods: Cutting-edge efforts like PII-Bench [3] and PII-Scope [4] are benchmarks for evaluating privacy-preserving systems or measuring data leakage risk, rather than detection algorithms for transformed text. Hence, their objectives diverge from ours.
2. Incompatible experimental setups and input requirements:  
These approaches rely on additional supervision or preprocessing that prevent fair comparisons with our general-purpose models.  
    - Require retraining with specific attack types: Methods like SeqAttack [5] and the triplet-loss-based work [6] rely on known attack patterns to generate adversarial examples for retraining or fine-tuning. These are supervised augmentation strategies intended to defend against “known” attacks, whereas our goal is to evaluate generalization in detection.  
    - Depend on text normalization preprocessing: Other methods, such as Silverspeak [7] and Eger [8], apply “restoration” or “denoising” preprocessing to transformed text. This forms a two-stage pipeline, making it impossible to independently and fairly assess the end-to-end detection capabilities of our models.
3. Limited applicability and generalization:  
Many of the reviewed algorithms are designed for specific types of transformations and cannot generalize to the diverse scenarios considered in our study. For instance, [8, 9] focus on homoglyph attacks; [10] targets glyph or homophone substitutions in Chinese; and [6] emphasizes typical spelling errors. These methods, while effective in their respective domains, cannot be generalized to the 21 heterogeneous format transformations included in DataSIR.

In summary, adapting these partially relevant methods for our evaluation would require extensive modifications, which in themselves may constitute an entirely separate line of research. More importantly, such comparisons would deviate from one of the core goals of our experimental design.

A central focus of our study is to validate that our dataset, DataSIR, can effectively distinguish between different levels of model recognition capability. To this end, we deliberately control the amount of prior knowledge provided to a single LLM via prompt design, enabling a clear and fair comparison across capability levels. Introducing fundamentally different algorithms and architectures would confound this setting, undermining the core conclusion that the observed performance differences stem from the dataset rather than the algorithmic choices.

Nevertheless, to address your concern and enhance the completeness of our paper, the following key revisions have been implemented:

+ In the Related Work section, we have added a new paragraph that systematically reviews and compares the aforementioned works, highlighting their differences in objectives, experimental setups, and application scope.  
+ In the Introduction, we explicitly emphasize that this study addresses a novel problem space that has not been adequately covered by existing research, thereby underscoring the necessity and contribution of our dataset.

We believe that these revisions will help clarify the positioning of our work and reinforce the case for its originality. Once again, we sincerely thank you for your insightful and constructive feedback.

[2] L. Li and X. Qiu. Tavat: token-aware virtual adversarial training for language understanding. 2020. 14543:118–168, 2004.

[3] H. Shen, Z. Gu, H. Hong, and W. Han. Pii-bench: Evaluating query-aware privacy protection systems. arXiv preprint arXiv:2502.18545, 2025. 

[4] K. K. Nakka, A. Frikha, R. Mendes, X. Jiang, and X. Zhou. Pii-scope: A comprehensive study on training data pii extraction attacks in llms. arXiv preprint arXiv:2410.06704, 2024.

[5] W. Simoncini and G. Spanakis. Seqattack: On adversarial attacks for named entity recognition. In Proceedings of the 2021 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing: System Demonstrations, pages 308–318, 2021. 

[6] C. Udomcharoenchaikit, P. Boonkwan, and P. Vateekul. Towards improving the robustness of sequential labeling models against typographical adversarial examples using triplet loss. Natural Language Engineering, 29(2):287–315, 2023. 

[7] Li, J., & Li, S. (2021). silverspeak. GitHub.

[8] S. Eger, G. G. Şahin, A. Rücklé, J.-U. Lee, C. Schulz, M. Mesgar, K. Swarnkar, E. Simpson, and I. Gurevych. Text processing like humans do: Visually attacking and shielding nlp systems. arXiv preprint arXiv:1903.11508, 2019. 

[9] J. Woodbridge, H. S. Anderson, A. Ahuja, and D. Grant. Detecting homoglyph attacks with a siamese neural network. In 2018 IEEE Security and Privacy Workshops (SPW), pages 22–28. IEEE, 2018.

[10] Z. Jiang, Z. Gao, G. He, Y. Kang, C. Sun, Q. Zhang, L. Si, and X. Liu. Detect camouflaged spam content via stoneskipping: Graph and text joint embedding for chinese character variation representation. arXiv preprint arXiv:1908.11561, 2019.



**Dataset Code Comments:** 

Sec. 4.2 and Sec. 4.3 lack sufficient detail regarding the experimental setup.

For the NLP models, the paper does not specify the versions of the external packages used, nor does it document the hyperparameter configurations.

For the LLMs, aside from mentioning that the temperature is set to 0, no other decoding parameters and prompts used are reported.

Providing a complete and transparent description of the experimental setup is crucial for reproducibility.

**Response to "Dataset Code Comments":**

International dialing codes (+86) may include or exclude parentheses and the '+' sign.”_
>

In addition, DataSIR also includes examples of other types of sensitive data categories that exhibit diverse representations across countries and regions, as shown in the table below:

summary.value: This paper introduces DataSIR, a benchmark dataset designed to evaluate sensitive information recognition (SIR) models under adversarial conditions. It includes 26 sensitive data categories based on major international regulations and applies 21 real-world format transformation techniques to generate over 1.6 million samples. The authors benchmark both traditional NLP tools and LLMs, showing that LLMs significantly outperform existing tools in recognizing transformed sensitive data. The dataset aims to support future research in robust SIR and adversarial defense.

strengths_contributions.value:
- The paper addresses a timely and underexplored problem in sensitive information recognition (SIR): the lack of robustness against real-world format transformation attacks.
- The evaluation is well-structured and comparative, covering both traditional NLP pipelines (e.g., HanLP, spaCy, Presidio) and modern LLMs (GPT-4, Gemini, DeepSeek), under prompt settings of varying informativeness.
- The paper is clearly written and well-organized. The dataset and code are fully open-sourced (Kaggle and GitHub), and implementation details are sufficient for reproducibility (Sec. 3.1, Sec. 4).

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- The paper primarily aggregates existing transformation techniques without introducing fundamentally new detection methods or modeling strategies. While the dataset is valuable, the contribution is more infrastructural than methodological, lacking novel algorithms or theoretical insights into SIR under evasion attacks.
- Evaluation focuses solely on recognition accuracy (LRAcc/DRAcc), without considering precision-recall balance, error types, or robustness curves. This limits interpretability and fails to reflect practical performance trade-offs, especially in real-world data leak prevention where false positives carry operational cost.
- All samples are presented as isolated phrases, ignoring critical context that often determines sensitivity (e.g., “John” as patient vs. doctor). This severely limits the dataset’s realism and utility for downstream SIR tasks that rely on contextual cues for correct classification.
- The 21 format transformations are treated uniformly, without a structured taxonomy based on semantic preservation, reversibility, or attack complexity. This prevents systematic analysis of model failure modes and undermines the dataset’s potential as a diagnostic benchmark.

summary.value: In this paper, the authors focus on the task of sensitive information recognition (SIR). The motivation of this work is two-folded: first, existing data leakage prevention techniques are insufficient against existing evasion techniques. Furthermore, current datasets cannot fully reflect real-world adversarial transformations, which is a roadblock toward the development of more effective SIR models. The authors then propose the DataSIR benchmark dataset, which is of large scale and includes several international regulations. Experimental results on adversarially augmented version of DataSIR further validate the value of this benchmark dataset.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The paper is clearly motivated by the importance of robust SIR in real-world scenarios, especially under format-based data leakage. The limitations of existing dataset including limited coverage of regulatory and transformation are also clearly stated in Section 1-2.
2. The paper is easy to follow thanks to the helpful flowchart (Figure 1) that outlines the overall pipeline from dataset construction to evaluation.
3. The dataset is evaluated using a wide range of models including:
    1). Four traditional NLP tools,
    2). Four LLMs varied prompt settings,
which strongly support the compatibility of this dataset with different scale of models. Moreover, the inclusion of diverse adversarial transformations and regulations ensures that the benchmark realistically captures the challenges , making it a valuable touchstone for SIR model development.

limitations_weaknesses.value: The format transformations are extensive and thoughtfully designed. However, the current description is not convincing enough for the realism of these transformations. It could strengthen the work to either provide more evidence of their practical relevance or consider incorporating more naturally occurring transformations.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

final_justification.value: The authors solved most of my concerns and I plan to maintain my original rating.

strengths_contributions.value:

limitations_weaknesses.value:

1. Line 86-88: Referring to each cited work simply as "dataset" feels imprecies. It would be appropriate to use the citation itself as the subject.
2. Line 271: There is a missing space that should be corrected.

The current version only evaluates existing open-source packages and models (both open- and closed-source). title.value: DataSIR: A Benchmark Dataset for Sensitive Information Recognition

TLDR.value: DataSIR, a multi-format sensitive information benchmark dataset, including 1,647,501 samples, designed to evaluate the performance of different models in recognizing sensitive information under evolving data leakage techniques.

abstract.value: With the rapid development of artificial intelligence technologies, the demand for training data has surged, exacerbating risks of data leakage. Despite increasing incidents and costs associated with such leaks, data leakage prevention (DLP) technologies lag behind evolving evasion techniques that bypass existing sensitive information recognition (SIR) models. Current datasets lack comprehensive coverage of these adversarial transformations, limiting the evaluation of robust SIR systems. To address this gap, we introduce DataSIR, a benchmark dataset specifically designed to evaluate SIR models on sensitive data subjected to diverse format transformations. We curate 26 sensitive data categories based on multiple international regulations, and collect 131,890 original samples correspondingly. Through empirical analysis of real-world evasion tactics, we implement 21 format transformation methods, which are applied to the original samples, expanding the dataset to 1,647,501 samples to simulate adversarial scenarios. We evaluated DataSIR using four traditional NLP models and four large language models (LLMs). For LLMs, we design structured prompts with varying degrees of contextual hints to assess the impact of prior knowledge on recognition accuracy. These evaluations demonstrate that our dataset effectively differentiates the performance of various SIR algorithms. Combined with its rich category and format diversity, the dataset can serve as a benchmark for evaluating related models and help develop future more advanced SIR models. Our dataset and experimental code are publicly available at https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/fanmo1/datasir and https://github.com/Fan-Mo-ZJU/DataSIR.
